- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] No optimistic UI confirmation is permitted anywhere in the client for outcome-affecting actions (accept, release, complete); an explicit 'sending / awaiting confirmation' transitional state must appear between user tap and server acknowledgment, even for a fraction of a second.
  rationale: The product's entire value proposition is that 'confirmed' means the server has actually arbitrated the outcome; a premature optimistic success flash before server ack would recreate the exact false-confidence failure mode the app exists to eliminate from group chats.
  rejected: Optimistic UI updates for responsiveness, reconciled after the fact with backend state
  constraints: This is a hard constraint on the API contract and client state machine in the next (architecture) phase, not a polish item
- [DEC-next_steps_small-001] The MVP slice for pulse-relay is the entire core loop end-to-end (post, live visibility + push, accept-race arbitration, release/reopen, still-open escalation, complete, audit/receipt) run by two real seeded accounts in one pod — not a stripped-down subset of it.
  rationale: The app has no secondary value proposition to fall back on; a subset that omits race arbitration, release, or still-open escalation is a different, less defensible app that happens to share a name, not a smaller version of pulse-relay.
  rejected: A smaller slice covering only post-and-accept without race arbitration, release, or still-open escalation; Treating this slice as a screen-by-screen build target rather than one complete incident workflow
  constraints: Later build phases must implement this slice as one continuous workflow tested with two real accounts, not as isolated screens
- [DEC-next_steps_small-002] The accept-race 'already covered by [name]' loser transition is locked as critical-path, non-negotiable-quality UX within this MVP slice, prioritized above other visual work in the slice including the shareable receipt card — it is explicitly carved out of the 'polish-only UI' cut bucket.
  rationale: This is the one moment in the product where 'you didn't get what you tapped for' is the correct, desired outcome, and a generic error-style treatment would read as the app malfunctioning rather than working as designed, directly undermining the trust the whole concept depends on.
  rejected: Treating the loser-state transition as an equal-priority correctness item alongside all other MVP screens, with visual treatment decided later as generic polish; Bundling this transition into the same cut-list tier as animations, theming, and iconography
  constraints: The next design phase must name this transition explicitly and not lump it into generic 'polish' decisions; Build priority within this slice puts this transition's fidelity ahead of receipt-card visual investment
- [DEC-next_steps_small-003] This MVP slice must use real server-side compare-and-swap arbitration and real APNs-delivered push notifications for the accept-race outcome; polling or client-side arbitration is explicitly disallowed as a stand-in, even if it would satisfy the same UI-state acceptance checklist.
  rationale: A polling-based or client-arbitrated version could pass every listed UI-state test while quietly failing to prove the backend is genuinely load-bearing, which is exactly the failure mode DEC-prompt_contract-004 and DEC-prompt_contract-008 exist to prevent, and would leave the 'push notifications driven by server-side events' backend justification from the original prompt unproven.
  rejected: Allowing a polling loop or client-side arbitration to stand in for real-time delivery during this slice, deferring real APNs wiring to a later phase
  constraints: The build phase's server-side write for accept must be a genuine conditional/compare-and-swap operation, and the winner/loser split must be sourced from that write's result, not inferred client-side; Push delivery in this slice must be real APNs with a working deep link, not simulated or polled
- [DEC-next_steps_small-004] The acceptance bar for this slice is a literal two-phone side-by-side demo — two real seeded accounts on two real devices where one confirms and the other shows 'already covered by [name]' within a second or two, with zero chat and zero manual reconciliation — with all itemized validation criteria (backend reachability, race-test determinism, push timing, release/reopen timing, still-open aging, force-quit persistence) serving as constituent checks within that demo rather than a separate competing checklist.
  rationale: A spec can pass every itemized criterion in isolation and still fail to produce the 'oh, that's clever' reaction if the pieces don't come together smoothly; naming the physical two-phone demo as the real bar keeps the team focused on the experience the whole concept depends on, not just checkbox completion.
  rejected: Treating the itemized validation criteria as a flat checklist with no single unifying acceptance demo
  constraints: Verification in the build phase should be run and judged as this literal two-device demo, with the itemized criteria checked as part of it
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The client shows honest, literal delivery-count copy on post ('Sent to N pod members') based on actual push registration/token status, with a warning banner if delivery looks uncertain, rather than implying full pod visibility.
  rationale: The free tier has no critical-alert/DND-bypass, so silent notification failure on a new pod's first incident is a real and likely failure mode; pretending otherwise would recreate the false-confidence problem this app exists to eliminate.
  rejected: Generic 'notification sent' copy that implies everyone was reached; Treating notification reliability as solvable in v1 and deferring the copy decision
  constraints: This must be documented as an accepted free-tier limitation, not treated as a bug to be silently patched later
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Same-day cutoffs and elapsed-time/aging calculations are computed entirely server-side using UTC timestamps plus a pod-home-timezone value set once at pod creation; no client-local-time logic is used for these calculations.
  rationale: Per-device local time creates ambiguous same-day boundaries and inconsistent aging displays across devices/timezones, undermining the 'no ambiguity, ever' requirement, especially for co-parenting pods with members in different timezones.
  rejected: Using device-local time to determine same-day cutoffs or elapsed time
  constraints: Pod home timezone must be captured at pod creation and used as the sole reference for date/aging math
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Every outcome-affecting action (post/accept/release/complete/withdraw) carries a client-generated idempotent action ID; the server must handle duplicate submissions idempotently, and any relaunch after a force-quit/crash must reconcile from server truth rather than trusting stale local UI state. A force-quit-mid-accept-before-ack scenario is a named acceptance test alongside the two-phone race demo.
  rationale: Without idempotency, retries or crash-relaunches during outcome-affecting actions could create duplicate requests or leave a device showing an outcome that never actually happened server-side, directly violating the no-false-confirmation principle.
  rejected: Leaving crash/retry behavior as an implementation detail discovered during build or QA
  constraints: This is a hard requirement on the API contract and client state machine in the architecture phase, not a polish item; The force-quit-mid-accept test case must be run and verified, not just described
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The pod-creator role gains exactly one additional capability beyond create-pod-and-get-code: revoke-and-reissue the join code, invalidating the old code immediately on rotation.
  rationale: A permanent, unrevocable join code would make the trust-graph-only matching safety property decorative if a code leaks or is sent to the wrong group; this is a narrow, surgical fix that doesn't reopen the admin-console scope already cut.
  rejected: Leaving join codes permanent and un-revocable; Building a full pod-admin console with member management to address this
  constraints: No other admin/moderation capability is added alongside this one
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] A pod with no members other than its creator gets a distinct empty state and CTA ('share the invite') that is visually and semantically separate from 'pod has other members but nobody has responded yet' (re-broadcast/escalate CTA).
  rationale: Collapsing these two very different situations into one generic 'waiting' state would recreate the false-confidence failure mode this app is built to eliminate, since a solo pod and an unresponsive pod require completely different next actions from the user.
  rejected: A single generic waiting/pending empty state covering both situations
  constraints: Design and build phases must treat these as two distinct, named UI states, not variants of the same screen
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The audit/receipt record persists after either party deletes their account, with the departed party rendered as a placeholder (e.g. 'Former member') in both the internal audit view and the shareable projection.
  rationale: The record may serve as custody/co-parenting documentation for the other party; allowing either party to unilaterally erase it via account deletion would undermine the entire evidence model the export feature was built to serve.
  rejected: Cascading deletion of the audit/receipt record when either party deletes their account
  constraints: Account deletion logic must explicitly exclude audit/receipt records from cascading deletes
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] UI copy and help text must explicitly state that an 'accepted' request means a trusted pod member has claimed responsibility, never that help or on-time arrival is guaranteed.
  rationale: Without this, users could reasonably infer a stronger guarantee than the app actually provides, especially since v1 has no location/ETA tracking to verify actual arrival.
  rejected: Leaving this distinction implicit and undocumented
  constraints: This must appear as visible copy on the accepted/claimed state, not just be an internal design assumption
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Add a first-class, requester-only terminal `withdrawn` state for same-day requests, usable only while the request is still open/still-open/reopened and unclaimed; it is arbitrated through the same server-side CAS mechanism as accept (so a race between an incoming accept and a withdraw resolves deterministically), triggers a real push/re-notify to the pod, and never generates an audit/receipt artifact. It is visually and semantically distinct from `complete` (e.g. muted/gray 'Withdrawn — no longer needed', not the green completion/receipt state).
  rationale: Without an explicit withdraw path, a self-resolved situation leaves a stale, actively-escalating open request that can lead a good-faith pod member to accept and act on a need that no longer exists — a real-world harm on par with the false-positive-confirmation risk the rest of the state machine is designed to prevent. Auto-closure alone doesn't cover the acute window before expiry kicks in.
  rejected: Relying solely on bounded auto-closure plus manual re-post, with no requester-facing withdraw action; Treating stale-request cleanup as a passive warning rather than an explicit requester-triggered state; Allowing a generic 'cancel' to behave like or be visually similar to a completed handoff
  constraints: `withdrawn` must never generate an audit/receipt artifact, since no handoff occurred; `withdrawn` must use a CAS-arbitrated write and idempotent action IDs like every other outcome-affecting action; `withdrawn` must be visually and copy-wise distinct from `complete` and `error` at the same fidelity bar as the 'already covered' transition
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The `withdrawn` and `release` actions are mutually exclusive by state: withdraw is only ever visible to the requester while the request is open/still-open (unclaimed); once a request is accepted, only the accepter's `release` action is available and withdraw disappears entirely.
  rationale: This eliminates the specific ambiguity risk that motivated hesitation about adding a cancel-like action — a user is never shown an action that could be misread as undoing someone else's commitment, because the two actions never coexist for the same request.
  rejected: Allowing withdraw to remain visible or available after a request has been accepted
  constraints: Client and server logic must enforce this mutual exclusivity as a state-machine invariant, not just a UI convention
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] V1 ships with no in-app moderation, reporting, muting, or member-removal capability to handle bad-faith or spam posting by a known pod member; this is an explicit, named, accepted limitation, mitigated only by trust-graph invite-only membership, per-request attribution/auditability, and the creator's code revoke/reissue capability.
  rationale: Building real moderation would reopen the admin-console/member-management scope deliberately cut in earlier phases for good reasons; leaving the risk undocumented would be worse than naming it plainly, consistent with how cold-start and Focus/DND limitations were handled.
  rejected: Adding member removal, reporting, or rate-limiting capability in v1; Leaving this risk unaddressed and undocumented
  constraints: Onboarding/help copy must state plainly that this is a trust-graph, invitation-based tool for known pods, not a moderated public platform; This limitation cannot be used to justify degrading any core-loop guarantee (APNs delivery, receipt integrity, state-machine correctness, four-state screens)
- [DEC-app_features-001] Must-have features are split into execution-priority tiers for build scheduling only: Tier-1 (auth persistence, zero-state create-or-join onboarding, no-PII posting with awaiting-confirmation, honest delivery-count copy, server-committed push dispatch, and CAS-based accept-race determinism) forms the literal two-phone demo and cannot be rushed; Tier-2 (release/reopen, withdrawn, still-open aging/re-broadcast, completion-to-receipt) remains fully required but may ship with rougher visual polish first if time is short.
  rationale: Both participants agreed the app has no fallback value proposition if the demo-critical race/notification path is wrong, so any time pressure must be absorbed by the less catastrophic parts of the loop, never the part that proves the backend is load-bearing.
  rejected: Treating all must-have features as equally weighted with no execution order; Making release/withdraw/still-open lower-priority in a way that could drop their correctness, not just their polish
  constraints: Tier-2 items remain required outcomes in the graded contract, not optional; Only visual/UX polish may be reduced under time pressure, never state-machine or server-invariant correctness
- [DEC-app_features-002] Subscription-tier features (multi-pod membership, exportable/signed receipt history, critical-alert notification bypass) are explicitly out of implementation scope for this build: no StoreKit integration, no paywall UI, no core behavior gated behind entitlement.
  rationale: Building paid-tier scaffolding does not increase confidence that the core trust-graph relay works under real concurrent pressure, and would divert time from the one thing this build must prove — real backend-load-bearing, two-device race correctness.
  rejected: Implementing paywall/subscription screens or entitlement checks in this build; Treating the three unlocks as hidden must-have build tasks
  constraints: Any schema entitlement fields must remain inert and unused in this build; No UI may reference or imply an unavailable premium flow
- [DEC-app_features-003] Tiering is strictly a scheduling/finish-quality mechanism, not a requirements-erosion mechanism: every must-have requirement remains required for acceptance, and all core invariants (CAS arbitration, idempotency, withdraw/release state exclusivity, four-state visibility, server-owned time semantics, no-optimistic terminal confirmation) must be implemented and testable regardless of tier.
  rationale: Prevents a build agent from reading the tiering as license to ship an incomplete or UI-only version of a 'lower tier' state transition under time pressure.
  rejected: Allowing partial or cosmetic-only implementations of core invariants for Tier-2 items when time is short
  constraints: A build that preserves UI layout for a Tier-2 screen but drops or fakes its underlying state transition is non-compliant, regardless of tier
- [DEC-app_features-004] The tokenized Theme.swift system and full light/dark coverage on every core screen is locked as a hard must-have with design-lint parity — no hardcoded font, size, spacing, or color literal outside the theme file, and no core-screen visual sign-off without both appearances verified.
  rationale: This fleet already has two recorded design-lint incidents matching exactly this failure (hardcoded font size, hardcoded inline color), and the global phase playbook already requires tokenized styling and dark-mode as a hard rule, not a stylistic nicety; leaving it on a 'should' list risked a build agent treating it as optional after spending its budget on core-loop correctness.
  rejected: Keeping the tokenized theme system on the should/could list; Allowing inline style literals in feature views with cleanup deferred; Treating dark-mode support as a later polish pass
  constraints: All core screens must reference Theme.swift for typography/color/spacing; Any screen with non-theme-sourced style literals is out of scope for acceptance
- [DEC-app_features-005] R-006, R-007, R-009, R-010, R-011, and R-037 are explicitly labeled demo-critical/uncuttable within the requirements contract itself: honest delivery-count copy, the server-side CAS/arbitration path, the deterministic winner/loser split, non-optimistic terminal confirmation, the bounded server-side push-dispatch commitment, and the literal two-device side-by-side demo.
  rationale: Under real schedule pressure a build agent can misjudge which corner is safe to cut; naming the safety-proof requirements explicitly in the document removes that judgment call rather than relying on inferred tiering alone.
  rejected: Relying on Tier-1/Tier-2 labeling alone to protect the safety-critical subset; Allowing any demo-critical requirement to be downgraded or softened under time pressure
  constraints: If any demo-critical requirement is incomplete, the build is non-compliant regardless of progress on Tier-2 items; Architecture and state-machine docs in later phases must carry these six requirements forward as explicitly non-negotiable
- [DEC-app_features-006] R-007 (push delivery) is locked as a two-part contract: the backend must commit the CAS write and submit the APNs payload within a strict server-owned bound (target <=2s happy-path), while actual device receipt timing is an empirically-observed property of the two-device demo, not a hard API-level pass/fail metric, given Apple's push infrastructure is best-effort.
  rationale: Prevents the requirements document from making an impossible-to-guarantee promise about third-party infrastructure while still holding the backend to strict, verifiable, server-side latency discipline.
  rejected: Wording the requirement as guaranteed/immediate end-to-end device delivery; Treating any observed APNs delay during the demo as an automatic backend defect
  constraints: Backend should target and log server-side dispatch timing as verifiable telemetry; Demo observations of infra-side delay are noted as delivery-UX risk, not treated as a false-positive architecture failure
- [DEC-design_discussion-001] The card status palette is locked as amber-pulse for open/awaiting/live requests, warm teal-green (not stoplight green) for confirmed/claimed, slate/muted gray for terminal non-actionable states (withdrawn, complete), with true red reserved exclusively for genuine system/network errors — never used for any normal product state including the accept-race loser.
  rationale: A parent glancing at this screen mid-panic reads color before text; using alarm-register colors (stoplight red/green, sci-fi HUD blue) for normal outcomes would misrepresent the emotional register the whole product promise depends on (relief, not alarm), and would risk the uncuttable already-covered transition reading as a malfunction.
  rejected: Literal stoplight red/green state coding; Cold blue-black sci-fi/military HUD palette with electric accents
  constraints: Theme.swift must define these as semantic color roles, not literals scattered through views; Red may never be used to render 'already covered by [name]' or any other non-error terminal state
- [DEC-design_discussion-002] The signature interaction is a pulse-to-latch motion: an open request card pulses on a calm heartbeat rhythm while awaiting server acknowledgment, then converts to a steady locked-panel state on resolution. Both the accept-race winner ('claimed/confirmed') and loser ('already covered by [name]') receive this same fast, mechanical, half-second latch treatment — no shake, no alert icon, no error styling on the loser.
  rationale: The losing side of the accept-race is the one moment in the product where 'you didn't get what you tapped for' is the correct, designed outcome (already flagged demo-critical/uncuttable in app_features); giving it the identical calm-latch treatment as the winner is what makes the two-phone demo read as 'the app worked' rather than 'the app broke' at a glance, without requiring the viewer to read any text.
  rejected: A plain status-chip text swap with no accompanying motion; Distinct/error-styled treatment for the losing transition (shake, alert icon, red accent)
  constraints: Reduce Motion must collapse the pulse/latch to an instant but still visually distinct crossfade, not remove the state distinction entirely; This transition's fidelity takes priority over all other visual polish in the build, per the earlier locked build-priority decisions
- [DEC-design_discussion-003] Default SwiftUI chrome is explicitly rejected: no plain List/Form rows, no default NavigationStack system-blue accents, and no transient toast-style confirmation (e.g. a flashing 'Accepted!' that disappears) for any outcome-affecting action.
  rationale: A row-list reads as an inbox and a vanishing toast is exactly the kind of easy-to-miss confirmation this app exists to eliminate; both would recreate the ambiguous-group-chat mental model the product is built to replace.
  rejected: Standard List/Form-based request feed with system accent color; Toast/alert-based confirmation for accept/release/complete/withdraw
  constraints: All outcome-affecting states must be persistent, baked into the card itself, sourced only from real backend acknowledgment
- [DEC-design_discussion-004] Screen scope stays deliberately narrow: session/auth gate, pod onboarding (create or join with true empty states), the live relay board, request composer, request detail (accept/release/withdraw), receipt, and minimal profile/pod-settings — no additional branching or surface area.
  rationale: Matches the build-priority guidance locked in portfolio_selection and app_features: this phase's entire purpose is eliminating claim/no-claim ambiguity, and any added screens or navigation branches would compete with that fidelity for build time.
  rejected: Adding richer navigation, tabs, or additional secondary screens at this stage
  constraints: Any future screen proposal must justify itself against directly reducing false-certainty or missed-coverage risk in the core loop
- [DEC-design_discussion-005] The design language's final name is 'Relay HUD.' The pulse-to-latch motion is the signature interaction within it, not a second brand name, and should be reflected in code as a concrete component name (e.g. BeaconCard/RelayBeaconView).
  rationale: A shorter, single name is what actually gets used in docs, code, and UI copy dozens of times through the build; 'Beacon' surviving as the literal name of the reusable motion component gives build agents a greppable identifier instead of a second competing brand term.
  rejected: 'Relay Beacon HUD' as the full product design-language name; Two parallel names (HUD for structure, Beacon for motion) with no clear precedence
  constraints: Design docs, Theme file comments, and onboarding copy should refer to the language as Relay HUD; The pulse-to-latch component should carry 'Beacon' in its SwiftUI type name
- [DEC-design_discussion-006] Secondary screens (receipt, profile/sign-out, pod settings/code rotation) inherit Theme tokens, spacing, typography, and state language but are explicitly barred from: custom entrance/exit transitions beyond the system default, bespoke empty-state illustration work (a plain SF Symbol plus one line of Theme-styled text is the ceiling), and any color treatment outside the shared semantic palette. The receipt card is a narrow exception only in that it gets a higher bar for typography and information hierarchy (since it leaves the app via the share sheet), but still receives no second signature animation.
  rationale: Turning 'utility-only' into named, specific bans prevents a build agent with spare time from investing craft budget into a secondary screen's own micro-interaction, which would come directly at the expense of the accept-race card's fidelity — the one thing this app is actually judged on.
  rejected: Leaving secondary-screen restraint as a soft 'keep it small' instruction with no named boundaries; Allowing the receipt card its own signature motion given its external-facing role
  constraints: Any secondary-screen work proposing custom motion or bespoke illustration is out of scope for this build; The receipt card's added craft budget is limited to typography/layout quality, not animation
- [DEC-design_discussion-007] The live board's default 'all clear' resting state — no open requests, quiet pod — is a real, composed screen: pod name, member count, an at-rest (non-pulsing) 'all clear' indicator using the same slate/teal semantic language, and the post-request CTA as the single obvious action. It does not get its own unique signature motion, but it must not be a blank view or a bare icon-plus-button placeholder.
  rationale: This is the single most-viewed screen in the app given pulse-relay's rare-but-critical usage pattern (named in round one as a core risk); an unfinished-looking resting state would make the whole app read as unfinished even if the high-stress states are polished, and directly violates the already-locked global rule that empty states are designed content, not blank views.
  rejected: Treating the resting state as a trivial placeholder screen since all design energy goes to the high-stress states; Giving the resting state its own signature motion, which would violate the secondary/non-critical-screen austerity principle
  constraints: The resting state must use the same Theme tokens and semantic palette as the active board, at rest rather than pulsing; This screen is exempt from the 'zero unique motion' secondary-screen rule only in that it needs real composed content, not in that it needs its own animation
- [DEC-design_discussion-008] If build time is constrained, visual/motion craft budget is spent in this strict order: (1) the open-to-awaiting pulse, (2) the deterministic winner/loser latch resolution, (3) completed/withdrawn terminal card clarity — with everything else (secondary screens, resting state) built plain and correct rather than polished.
  rationale: Names an explicit tiebreak so a build agent under deadline pressure doesn't have to guess where to cut visual finish, directly extending the Tier-1/Tier-2 execution-priority logic already locked in app_features into concrete design-craft terms.
  rejected: Leaving craft-budget prioritization implicit and inferred from the rest of this phase's output
  constraints: No craft time should go to secondary-screen polish before all three named priorities are fully realized
- [DEC-design_handoff-001] Codex's structured DESIGN SPEC (type scale, spacing grid, component inventory, navigation map, motion/haptics, accessibility) is adopted as the canonical base for this phase, extended with Claude's client-state-machine layer rather than replaced by a competing token set.
  rationale: Codex's pass was the more fully-worked-out formal document hitting every required playbook heading; Claude explicitly conceded this rather than defending her own alternate numbers, so rewriting from scratch would only create churn and regression risk in a constrained build.
  rejected: Maintaining two parallel token sets and reconciling per-value; Rewriting the spec around Claude's alternate type/spacing/color values
  constraints: Any further palette changes must be surgical edits to Codex's existing token file, not a wholesale replacement
- [DEC-design_handoff-002] The request/card state machine distinguishes awaitingConfirmation (this device's own action in flight) from reconciling (state learned via a push-triggered refetch) as separate internal states sharing the pulse visual, plus queuedOffline (action taken with no connection, not yet in flight) and a distinct 'no longer open' state for a deep-link that resolves to a withdrawn/expired request — all four folded into the formal per-screen spec, not left as an inferred edge case.
  rationale: Collapsing awaitingConfirmation and reconciling into one case would make the losing device in the accept-race snap straight to 'already covered' with no pulse, destroying the exact side-by-side visual proof the two-phone demo depends on; queuedOffline and the expired-deep-link state prevent false or scary-looking states for two situations (offline compose, stale notification taps) that will happen routinely in real use.
  rejected: Treating reconciling as the same internal case as awaitingConfirmation; Rendering a queued offline action as a generic awaiting-confirmation spinner; Rendering an expired/withdrawn deep-link target as a generic error state
  constraints: Build must implement all four as named, distinct internal states, not just visually similar variants of two states
- [DEC-design_handoff-003] Screen graph and navigation are locked: AppGate resolves to AuthGate, PodOnboarding, or RelayBoard (default root); RelayBoard presents RequestComposer and RequestDetail as sheets, with RequestDetail also serving as the push deep-link destination; Profile and PodSettings are reachable only via stack push from the board header. No tabs, no additional navigation branches.
  rationale: Matches the narrow-screen-scope discipline already locked in design_discussion and keeps the IA aligned with the app's actual single-core-loop workload rather than adding chrome for an app with essentially one screen that matters.
  rejected: A tab-based root; Additional top-level navigation branches beyond the core loop and two secondary screens
  constraints: No later phase may add tabs or additional root-level navigation destinations
- [DEC-design_handoff-004] Motion timing is locked: the open-to-awaiting pulse is a 0.9s ease-in-out repeating breathing animation (scale 0.99→1.02 plus border alpha oscillation); resolution to either winner or loser uses an identical 0.45s mechanical spring latch (response 0.45, damping 0.82); Reduce Motion collapses both to a ~0.15s crossfade that preserves the text/icon state change; haptics never differentiate winner from loser as success versus warning/error.
  rationale: Codifies design_discussion's requirement that the accept-race loser reads as 'worked as designed' rather than a malfunction, down to exact animation and haptic values a build agent can implement without inventing anything.
  rejected: Distinct or error-styled haptic/motion treatment for the losing transition
  constraints: No implementation may give the loser transition a different duration, curve, or haptic category than the winner
- [DEC-design_handoff-005] If build time is constrained, visual/motion craft effort is spent in this order: (1) the open-to-awaiting pulse, (2) the winner/loser latch resolution, (3) completed/withdrawn terminal card clarity — before any polish on the board resting state or secondary screens.
  rationale: Directly carries forward the craft-budget tiebreak already locked in design_discussion into this phase's concrete spec, so a build agent under deadline pressure has an explicit order rather than having to infer one.
  rejected: Leaving craft-budget priority unstated in this phase's own spec and relying solely on the prior phase's mention of it
  constraints: No craft time goes to secondary-screen or resting-state polish before all three named priorities are fully realized
- [DEC-design_handoff-007] The Relay HUD surface/neutral system is corrected to a warm-neutral palette (warm off-white backgrounds, warm charcoal dark surfaces) replacing the cool-blue scaffold from the earlier draft, while all state accent colors (amber pulse, teal confirmed, slate terminal, error red) remain unchanged.
  rationale: The neutral scaffolding, not the state accents, was the remaining source of the 'cold blue-black sci-fi HUD' register explicitly rejected in design_discussion's DEC-design_discussion-001; a cold base can trigger an alarm register even when state accents are correct.
  rejected: Keeping the blue-leaning neutral tokens on the grounds that state accents were already correct; Claude's independently-proposed alternate warm hex values, treated as confirming the same fix rather than a competing spec since both point the same direction
  constraints: All base surface/divider/background/card tones in Theme.swift must use the warm-neutral values in the final palette table; No non-tokenized neutral literals anywhere outside Theme.swift
- [DEC-design_handoff-008] Relay board request ordering is exclusively server-authoritative displayOrder (created-at ascending plus a deterministic backend tie-break); no client-side urgency computation or local re-sort exists anywhere in the spec.
  rationale: No urgency/severity/priority field exists anywhere in the locked data model; leaving 'urgency' in the spec language would hand a build agent an undefined sort key it would have to invent or silently drop, violating the playbook rule that no adjective may stand in for a number.
  rejected: Retaining 'sorted by urgency then age' as descriptive shorthand for age-driven sorting; Allowing client-side re-sorting as a fallback
  constraints: Board component renders request IDs in exact backend response order; Any future urgency concept requires an explicit new data-model decision in a later phase, not implicit inclusion here
- [DEC-design_handoff-009] Push notification payloads are never rendered as authoritative request state; every push is treated strictly as a wake-up signal that must trigger a targeted authoritative refetch of that specific request before any card transition occurs, and this is written as its own explicit architectural rule in the spec.
  rationale: Decoding and rendering directly from the notification payload is the fastest, most obvious implementation path for a competent iOS engineer, and it would pass every screenshot review and casual demo while silently breaking CAS correctness the first time APNs delivers pushes out of order or drops one — exactly the failure this app's core value proposition depends on not happening.

## Phase Purpose

Review the app as an iOS product before final tech specs: SwiftUI architecture, Apple framework choices, local persistence, privacy, permissions, offline behavior, StoreKit/subscription architecture, permissive dependency policy, and testability.

## Transcript


### Round 1


**Codex (Backend / Systems Engineer · Systems Thinker) — Round 1**

For this phase I would lock the iOS product architecture around a server-authoritative relay core with a very thin, deterministic SwiftUI client. The client should render from a local cache immediately, but every meaningful outcome state must come from a confirmed server write so we never show “covered”, “withdrawn”, “complete” or any terminal state without server proof.

I would pick a custom REST backend over third-party realtime frameworks because this use case needs strict state transitions, idempotent actions, and auditability. A good fit is Swift or Node as an API service backed by PostgreSQL, with one push-worker service per change and optional Redis lock cache only if needed. PostgreSQL is the critical piece because we need compare-and-swap-safe transitions (first-accept-wins, mutually exclusive release/withdraw state changes), stable pagination/order, and transactional write logs for receipts/evidence. I would keep the external contract simple and explicit: versioned `/api/v1` endpoints, strong DTOs, and deterministic responses. Core endpoints: auth bootstrap, `POST /pods`, `POST /pods/join`, `GET /pods/{podId}/state`, `POST /requests` with action IDs, `POST /requests/{id}/actions` for accept/release/complete/withdraw, and `GET /requests/{id}` for deep-link reconciliation, plus `/requests/{id}/receipt`. Every action endpoint must be idempotent and return either the updated request row or a conflict payload (“already covered”, “not open”, “stale”) and never silently succeed on duplicate retries.

On-device architecture should be two-layered: a pure domain/state layer (no network/UI dependencies) and a SwiftUI presentation layer. Use `Observation`/`ObservableObject` stores plus async repositories: one for session/auth, one for pod membership, one for request feed and outbox. Keep action execution in a command/reducer-like state machine that can express `queuedOffline`, `awaitingConfirmation`, `reconciling`, and the latched terminal states. This is where the two-phone proof lives, so state transitions should be testable as pure functions.

For local persistence, use SwiftData for cached board/request/receipt snapshots, queued outbox actions, and sync cursors, then Keychain for auth credentials/session refresh secrets. `URLSession` with `async/await` should be the network layer. Don’t add a network abstraction library: it’s unnecessary overhead and conflicts with the no-bloat direction. SwiftData is acceptable for app persistence under the target policy, and it gives us robust “cached continuity + freshness banner” behavior. Keep sensitive tokens in Keychain only, and avoid storing user-entered notes or member metadata beyond what is displayed; this product already avoids child identifiers and location.

Permissions should be intentionally minimal: Sign in with Apple (required), remote notifications (required), background remote notifications (recommended so push-triggered refetch can run when user taps or receives content-available wake), and optionally user-notification authorization at first feature touchpoint. There is no location, no photos, no contacts, no camera, no mic. For deep links, a custom URL scheme is simplest and avoids associated-domain work; if the team wants universal links later, add that later after baseline is stable. Privacy-by-design requirements should be explicit in API terms too: no child PII fields, no implied background checks, no trust badges unless real verification is performed, and placeholder member names only where needed.

Offline behavior must be first-class in architecture, not only in UI copy: maintain a durable action outbox in SwiftData with generated `client_action_id`, exponential retry with backoff, and idempotent replay against the server endpoint that enforces idempotency keys. On launch/foreground and after forced crash/quit, render stale cache first for continuity, then block high-confidence terminal display until freshness sync completes. A top-level board refresh banner is right here. If push is missing or delayed, explicit user-facing uncertainty copy should remain accurate rather than faking success.

Push architecture should be hard-coded into backend contract as wake-up-only: payload contains request/pod identifiers and event hints, never authoritative state. The client always refetches the request or pod slice before changing UI state. This avoids out-of-order push corruption and preserves CAS correctness.

For StoreKit/subscriptions: v1 should be explicitly non-monetized and include only placeholders for future fields. Do not add StoreKit 2 now; no entitlement checks, no paywall paths, no SKProduct calls. Keep the three future unlock ideas as schema placeholders if needed, but keep them inert and out of runtime behavior.

Dependency/license policy: keep iOS dependency surface to Apple frameworks and no prohibited packages. On the app: `AuthenticationServices`, `UserNotifications`, `BackgroundTasks` if needed, `SwiftData`, `OSLog`, `Combine`/`Observation`, `CryptoKit` if needed for signature checks. No Alamofire, no SwiftyJSON, no Realm, no third-party design systems. If backend needs one extra helper library, keep it small, actively maintained, and permissive (prefer Foundation-native/first-party where possible).

Test strategy should prioritize behavior failures, not cosmetic checks. Use protocol injection and pure state-mapper tests for the request FSM, acceptance race transitions, elapsed-time formatting, deep-link branching, and outbox replay semantics. Add parser tests for action/result decoding and a contract test around accept/release/withdraw CAS race outcomes. One UI smoke test should drive the core loop: seed two accounts in one pod, post request, race accept, observe deterministic winner/loser transition, release/reopen, withdraw, then receipt render. Anything less risks missing the core architecture proof.

Biggest objection to my own direction is APNs reliability and app lifecycle drift; server CAS is only half of the contract unless push-triggered refetch is implemented correctly and tested for stale/duplicate push behavior. The final phase output must preserve the non-negotiable invariant: no push payload ever directly drives terminal state, and no terminal outcome is shown without a validated server response.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Closer) — Round 1**

Here's my independent pass on this as the iOS product review, and I'm going to be blunt about where I think this spec has real gaps that will bite during build, not just where it's fine.

On architecture: root the app in a single `@Observable` (iOS 17+, matches the Swift Testing target already assumed elsewhere in this fleet's playbook) `AppSession` object that owns exactly one source of truth — auth state, current pod, and the board's request list — and drive `AppGate`'s three-way routing off that object rather than scattering `@State` across views. Every `BeaconCard` state transition described in design_handoff (openUnclaimed, awaitingConfirmation, queuedOffline, reconciling, latchedConfirmed, latchedAlreadyCovered, reopened, stillOpen, withdrawn, completed, error) needs to live as an actual Swift enum with associated data, not a string or a set of booleans — if it's booleans, someone will eventually construct an illegal combination (e.g. `awaitingConfirmation && queuedOffline` both true) and that illegal state is exactly the kind of bug that silently breaks the two-phone demo. I'd put the whole request state machine behind a `RequestSyncCoordinator` actor, not a plain class — this is the piece that receives push wake-ups, fires the authoritative refetch, replays the offline outbox, and resolves reconciling vs. awaitingConfirmation, and if it's not an actor you will get data races the first time a push arrives while a local action is also in flight, which is a normal, not edge-case, timing scenario for this app.

Frameworks: URLSession with async/await for all networking, Codable for the wire format, AuthenticationServices for Sign in with Apple, UserNotifications + APNs for push, SwiftData for the local cache/outbox, OSLog for logging, Keychain Services (via a thin wrapper, not raw C API calls scattered around) for the session token — not SwiftData, not UserDefaults. That last one is a concrete risk nobody's named yet: the app's own locked requirement is that push arrival triggers a background refetch, but if the Keychain item's accessibility is the default (`whenUnlocked`), a push that arrives while the phone is locked can't authenticate that refetch, and the app will silently fail to reconcile exactly when it matters most — a parent's phone is locked in their pocket when the push lands. Use `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly` explicitly and say so in the spec, or this is a guaranteed field failure. No WebSocket library and no persistent socket anywhere — the architecture is REST plus APNs-triggered refetch, which is also the reason zero third-party networking dependencies are needed at all.

Persistence: SwiftData holds Pod, Request (mirroring server state plus the local-only enum wrapper), and OutboxAction (client-generated idempotent action ID, action type, payload, created-at, retry count) — but I want this explicitly declared as a disposable cache, not a durable store with its own migration story. Cloud is the sole source of truth for arbitration per the product brief, so on any schema mismatch between app versions, the correct and far cheaper move is: wipe the local SwiftData store, keep the Keychain token, and refetch fresh from the server — not a hand-rolled lightweight migration plan. If we don't decide that now, someone will spend build time on SwiftData migrations for a cache that doesn't need them.

Permissions and privacy: no location, no contacts, no photo library, no camera — nothing here forces a permission dialog except notifications and Sign in with Apple's implicit account flow, and that's good, it keeps the permission surface small and honest. But push permission timing matters and isn't in the spec yet — request it after pod join succeeds and before the user's first compose/accept action, with a one-line primer explaining why ("Pod members need to reach you the moment someone needs pickup help"), not at cold launch before the user has any reason to say yes; a denied prompt at launch is very hard to recover from since re-prompting requires a Settings deep-link, and this app's entire value proposition depends on that permission being granted. Flag now, not later: the "critical-alert-tier notification that bypasses Focus/DND" subscription feature requires Apple's Critical Alerts entitlement, which Apple grants selectively and has historically reserved for health/safety/security use cases — there's real feasibility risk that a childcare-coordination app doesn't get approved for it, and since it's already deferred out of v1 implementation, I'd explicitly note that its future feasibility is unproven, not assumed. Also: no inline "Accept" action button on the lock-screen notification — tapping the notification should only deep-link into RequestDetail through the normal reconciling path. A notification action button that fires an API call directly from the notification center would be a side door around the entire no-optimistic-UI rule this app is built on, and it's exactly the kind of shortcut a build agent takes because UNNotificationAction makes it trivially easy. A PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy manifest is required for App Store submission given SwiftData/Keychain/timestamp API usage — this needs to exist, not be discovered at submission time. StoreKit: zero implementation, no paywall, entitlement field present in the schema but unused and unreferenced by any UI, exactly as already locked — I'm not reopening that.

Dependency and license decision: zero third-party dependencies for this build. Every requirement — networking, JSON, persistence, push registration, Sign in with Apple, background refresh, logging — is covered by first-party frameworks, which trivially satisfies the permissive-license policy by not needing it at all. If a future phase proposes a dependency, the bar should be "does this materially reduce risk on the CAS/push path specifically," not general convenience.

Testing: the highest-value unit tests are the request state machine transitions (assert that a push-triggered reconcile never collapses into awaitingConfirmation, that an incoming accept while a withdraw is in flight resolves to exactly one outcome), the offline outbox replay ordering, and the same-day/UTC cutoff math against the pod's home timezone — all pure logic, all Swift Testing, all fast. Persistence round-trip tests for the SwiftData models and a Codable mapper test against fixed JSON fixtures via a stubbed URLProtocol, never a real network call in unit tests. The one thing I want to say clearly because I think it'll otherwise get missed: a standard XCUITest can't validate the actual accept-race, because it drives one app instance — the CAS correctness claim needs its own integration test that fires two concurrent accept requests at a test backend instance and asserts exactly one 200 and one "already claimed" response, independent of and in addition to the manual two-device demo. Treat the manual two-phone demo as the acceptance bar for the experience, and this concurrent-integration test as the acceptance bar for the mechanism — passing one without the other isn't good enough, since a flaky manual demo could pass by luck and a mechanically-sound backend could still fail a rushed UI wiring.

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

Looking at round 1, both Codex and Claude landed on the same overall shape — server-authoritative REST + PostgreSQL backend, thin deterministic SwiftUI client, push-as-wake-up-only (never trusted as state), SwiftData for local cache/outbox, Keychain for auth, zero third-party dependencies, no StoreKit in v1, minimal permissions (no location/contacts/photos/camera). That's real agreement on the architecture's spine.

But Claude's pass wasn't just a restatement — she added a batch of specific, concrete decisions that Codex hasn't had a chance to respond to yet: an actor-based `RequestSyncCoordinator` (instead of a plain class) to avoid data races when a push arrives mid local-action; an enum-based state machine instead of booleans (to prevent illegal state combinations); a specific Keychain accessibility flag (`kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly`) needed so a locked-phone push can still authenticate a background refetch; push-permission request timing (after pod join, with a primer — not at cold launch); an explicit ban on notification action buttons (deep-link only, no side-door API calls from the notification center); a flag that the Critical Alerts entitlement (needed for the deferred DND-bypass subscription feature) may not even be grantable to this app category; a `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` manifest requirement; treating SwiftData as a wipe-and-refetch disposable cache rather than something with its own migration story; and a concurrent-integration test (two simultaneous accept requests against a real test backend) as a mechanism-level acceptance bar distinct from the manual two-phone demo.

None of this contradicts Codex's proposal — it's mostly sharpening real gaps — but it hasn't been confirmed or pushed back on yet, so I don't think this phase is done.

First, `RequestSyncCoordinator` as an actor is mandatory for this phase, not optional. You already have two asynchronous producers (local action flow + push wake/refetch) that can mutate the same in-memory request view at the same time; if that coordinator isn’t an actor, you’re one race away from impossible UI states. On top of that, all card phases (`openUnclaimed`, `awaitingConfirmation`, `queuedOffline`, `reconciling`, etc.) should be a single `enum` in one place, not booleans, because the invariant that `queuedOffline` and `awaitingConfirmation` are mutually exclusive is only enforceable if the type system carries it for you. I’d even make transitions deterministic via a pure reducer so unit tests can prove “only one terminal transition path per action sequence.”

On permissions, Claude’s call is exactly right: request push authorization only when it becomes relevant (after authenticated + pod is established), and with one clear rationale line before the prompt. Remote-notification permission and APNs token registration should exist before first publish from a pod member; asking later than that risks misses, asking too early risks a dead-end denial. Also, no notification action buttons on this first implementation. Deep-link only, then authoritative refetch. Any side-channel action from Notification Center is a silent bypass of the no-optimistic-confirmation contract and is the same class of bug this app is designed to avoid.

Keychain accessibility is one of those low-level details that saves or sinks demos: use `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly` (or equivalent in your helper) for session refresh tokens so a locked-phone push wake can still authenticate a fetch. Also do not over-invest in background entitlement complexity; make the push wake path best-effort and always recover with foreground poll-on-open.

I agree with deferring the Critical Alerts entitlement entirely for v1 and explicitly marking it as uncertain for a childcare-coordination product. If this were truly critical in v2, we should re-open feasibility with Apple’s approval rules first and only then wire entitlement and user-facing semantics. For v1, keep it out of runtime logic entirely.

For persistence, I support SwiftData, but I’d refine “disposable cache” to avoid undermining reliability. Treat board/request snapshots as cache-only with “invalidate on schema mismatch” behavior, but keep outbox action records durable enough to survive app relaunches (and ideally migration hiccups). If you do hard-reset local store, do it in a way that does not drop unsent user-intent actions silently; either preserve outbox separately before purge or fail-safe into an explicit recovery flow. Since we’re optimizing for correctness, losing queued actions after an upgrade is worse than losing stale cache.
  
On testing, I strongly accept adding a real concurrent server integration test: two simultaneous accepts against a seeded request must return exactly one success and one deterministic conflict before any UI pass is accepted. Keep manual two-device demo as behavioral acceptance, but make the backend mechanism test executable and machine-verified. The actor-based coordinator and the enum state machine are the same underlying claim — state must be structurally impossible to corrupt, not just conventionally correct. An actor gives you serialized access to that state by construction. I'm calling this locked unless someone gives me a concrete reason an actor doesn't work here, and I haven't heard one.

Keychain accessibility — this one I actually want to raise the stakes on, because I don't think either of us fully worked through the failure mode last round. If the token's accessibility is `whenUnlocked` (the default most engineers reach for without thinking) and a push arrives while the phone is locked, the background refetch that's supposed to authenticate that push and resolve reconciling will fail — not with a clear error, but silently, because the OS just won't let the process read the Keychain item yet. That means the exact moment this app's core value proposition is supposed to fire — "the other pod member already claimed this, don't worry" arriving instantly on your lock screen — is the exact moment it's most likely to quietly not update, and the user won't find out until they unlock the phone and open the app, which defeats the entire "flawless first incident" bar from per_app_product_brief. `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly` is the fix and it's a one-line decision. I want this named in the phase output as an explicit constraint on the Keychain wrapper, not left as an implementation detail someone infers correctly or doesn't.

## Final Output

**SwiftUI architecture:** Root the app in a single `@Observable` `AppSession` (auth + current pod + board state) driving `AppGate`'s three-way routing (AuthGate / PodOnboarding / RelayBoard). All request-card state transitions are owned by an actor-based `RequestSyncCoordinator` — the sole mutator of request state, receiving both local-action results and push-triggered refetches, so the two concurrent producers (a user's own tap, and a push wake-up) can never race into an illegal combined state. Card state is a single Swift enum with associated data (`openUnclaimed`, `awaitingConfirmation`, `queuedOffline`, `reconciling`, `latchedConfirmed`, `latchedAlreadyCovered`, `reopened`, `stillOpen`, `withdrawn`, `completed`, `error`) driven through a pure, unit-testable reducer — never booleans.

**Backend:** Custom REST API (`/api/v1`) over PostgreSQL, chosen specifically because the product needs compare-and-swap-safe transitions (first-accept-wins, mutually exclusive release/withdraw), transactional audit/receipt writes, and stable ordering — not a generic BaaS/realtime framework. Every outcome-affecting endpoint (accept/release/withdraw/complete) takes a client-generated idempotent action ID and returns either the updated row or an explicit conflict payload, never a silent success on retry. Push (APNs) is architecturally a wake-up signal only — payload never rendered as state; the client always authoritatively refetches before transitioning any card.

**Apple frameworks:** URLSession + async/await (networking), Codable (wire format), SwiftData (local cache + outbox), Keychain Services via a thin wrapper (session credentials — `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly`), AuthenticationServices (Sign in with Apple), UserNotifications/APNs (push, deep-link only, no notification action buttons), OSLog (logging), Observation/Combine for state. No WebSocket library, no persistent socket.

**Persistence:** SwiftData holds Pod/Request/Receipt snapshots as a disposable, cache-only mirror of server truth (purge-and-refetch on schema mismatch, no hand-rolled migration plan), plus a durable outbox of queued offline actions that must survive relaunch/upgrade without silent loss — if a hard reset of the cache is ever needed, the outbox is preserved or the user is routed into an explicit recovery flow, never silently dropped. On launch/foreground and after force-quit mid-action, stale cache renders immediately for continuity behind a top-level syncing banner; no terminal state is shown with full confidence before the first fresh fetch lands.

**Permissions/privacy:** Only Sign in with Apple and remote-notification authorization — no location, contacts, photos, or camera. Notification permission is requested after authenticated pod membership is established, with a one-line rationale, not at cold launch. The real reconciliation trigger is a visible alert push plus tap-deep-link or foreground/background-transition refetch; silent content-available push is a best-effort bonus only, never relied on as the primary path. Critical Alerts (needed for the already-deferred DND-bypass subscription feature) stays fully unimplemented in v1 and is explicitly flagged as feasibility-uncertain for a childcare-coordination app, not assumed obtainable. A `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` manifest is required given SwiftData/Keychain/timestamp API usage.

**Dependency/license decision:** Zero third-party dependencies. Every requirement (networking, JSON, persistence, push, auth, logging) is covered by first-party Apple frameworks; no Alamofire/SwiftyJSON/Realm or equivalents, satisfying the permissive-license policy by not needing an exception at all. No ML/LLM/AR stack in v1.

**Testing implications:** Pure unit tests for the reducer/state machine (proving reconciling never collapses into awaitingConfirmation, mutual exclusivity of queuedOffline/awaitingConfirmation, offline outbox replay ordering, UTC same-day cutoff math), Codable mapper tests against fixed JSON fixtures via stubbed `URLProtocol` (no real network in unit tests), SwiftData round-trip tests. Two acceptance tiers, both required: (1) a backend-level concurrent integration test with no UI — two simultaneous accept calls against a real test instance of the CAS endpoint must deterministically return exactly one success and one conflict, plus a companion accept-vs-withdraw race test — proving the mechanism; (2) the manual two-phone demo — proving the experience. Passing only one is not sufficient.

## Final Output

**SwiftUI architecture:** Root the app in a single `@Observable` `AppSession` (auth + current pod + board state) driving `AppGate`'s three-way routing (AuthGate / PodOnboarding / RelayBoard). All request-card state transitions are owned by an actor-based `RequestSyncCoordinator` — the sole mutator of request state, receiving both local-action results and push-triggered refetches, so the two concurrent producers (a user's own tap, and a push wake-up) can never race into an illegal combined state. Card state is a single Swift enum with associated data (`openUnclaimed`, `awaitingConfirmation`, `queuedOffline`, `reconciling`, `latchedConfirmed`, `latchedAlreadyCovered`, `reopened`, `stillOpen`, `withdrawn`, `completed`, `error`) driven through a pure, unit-testable reducer — never booleans.

**Backend:** Custom REST API (`/api/v1`) over PostgreSQL, chosen specifically because the product needs compare-and-swap-safe transitions (first-accept-wins, mutually exclusive release/withdraw), transactional audit/receipt writes, and stable ordering — not a generic BaaS/realtime framework. Every outcome-affecting endpoint (accept/release/withdraw/complete) takes a client-generated idempotent action ID and returns either the updated row or an explicit conflict payload, never a silent success on retry. Push (APNs) is architecturally a wake-up signal only — payload never rendered as state; the client always authoritatively refetches before transitioning any card.

**Apple frameworks:** URLSession + async/await (networking), Codable (wire format), SwiftData (local cache + outbox), Keychain Services via a thin wrapper (session credentials — `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly`), AuthenticationServices (Sign in with Apple), UserNotifications/APNs (push, deep-link only, no notification action buttons), OSLog (logging), Observation/Combine for state. No WebSocket library, no persistent socket.

**Persistence:** SwiftData holds Pod/Request/Receipt snapshots as a disposable, cache-only mirror of server truth (purge-and-refetch on schema mismatch, no hand-rolled migration plan), plus a durable outbox of queued offline actions that must survive relaunch/upgrade without silent loss — if a hard reset of the cache is ever needed, the outbox is preserved or the user is routed into an explicit recovery flow, never silently dropped. On launch/foreground and after force-quit mid-action, stale cache renders immediately for continuity behind a top-level syncing banner; no terminal state is shown with full confidence before the first fresh fetch lands.

**Permissions/privacy:** Only Sign in with Apple and remote-notification authorization — no location, contacts, photos, or camera. Notification permission is requested after authenticated pod membership is established, with a one-line rationale, not at cold launch. The real reconciliation trigger is a visible alert push plus tap-deep-link or foreground/background-transition refetch; silent content-available push is a best-effort bonus only, never relied on as the primary path. Critical Alerts (needed for the already-deferred DND-bypass subscription feature) stays fully unimplemented in v1 and is explicitly flagged as feasibility-uncertain for a childcare-coordination app, not assumed obtainable. A `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` manifest is required given SwiftData/Keychain/timestamp API usage.

**Dependency/license decision:** Zero third-party dependencies. Every requirement (networking, JSON, persistence, push, auth, logging) is covered by first-party Apple frameworks; no Alamofire/SwiftyJSON/Realm or equivalents, satisfying the permissive-license policy by not needing an exception at all. No ML/LLM/AR stack in v1.

**Testing implications:** Pure unit tests for the reducer/state machine (proving reconciling never collapses into awaitingConfirmation, mutual exclusivity of queuedOffline/awaitingConfirmation, offline outbox replay ordering, UTC same-day cutoff math), Codable mapper tests against fixed JSON fixtures via stubbed `URLProtocol` (no real network in unit tests), SwiftData round-trip tests. Two acceptance tiers, both required: (1) a backend-level concurrent integration test with no UI — two simultaneous accept calls against a real test instance of the CAS endpoint must deterministically return exactly one success and one conflict, plus a companion accept-vs-withdraw race test — proving the mechanism; (2) the manual two-phone demo — proving the experience. Passing only one is not sufficient.

----- Testing And Quality -----
# Testing & Quality for a Small iOS App

Target: **iOS 17+ deployment / Swift 5.9+**, built with **Xcode 16 or later** (Swift Testing ships in-box; use `OS=latest` in CI so the simulator version tracks your toolchain). Zero third-party deps — everything here is Apple first-party. This is a pragmatic reference for an AI building a prototype: maximize confidence per line of test code, avoid brittle tests that break on every UI tweak.

---

## TL;DR strategy for a prototype

- **Don't chase coverage.** Test the code that would be embarrassing or expensive if wrong: money math, date logic, parsing, persistence round-trips, state machines, reducers/view models.
- **Skip testing SwiftUI view bodies.** Use **Xcode Previews** as your visual feedback loop instead — they are faster than any UI test.
- **Make logic testable by moving it out of views** into plain `struct`/`class` types with injected dependencies. If it's testable, it's usually also better architected.
- **One happy-path UI test** through the primary flow catches wiring/regression bugs that unit tests can't. More than a handful of UI tests is usually a net negative for a prototype (slow, flaky).
- **Prefer Swift Testing (`@Test`)** for new unit tests. Keep XCTest for **UI tests** (`XCUIApplication`) and **performance tests** (`measure`) — those APIs are XCTest-only.

Priority order to write tests, highest first:
1. Pure logic with branches (pricing, validation, formatting, sorting/filtering).
2. View model / reducer state transitions (given input → expected observable state).
3. Persistence & serialization round-trips (Codable, SwiftData/UserDefaults).
4. Networking mappers (raw JSON → domain model), with a fake session — never hit the real network.
5. One end-to-end UI smoke test of the core flow.

---

## Project setup

- **Unit test target**: File ▸ New ▸ Target ▸ *Unit Testing Bundle*. Choose **Swift Testing** (default in Xcode 16+) or XCTest.
- **UI test target**: separate *UI Testing Bundle* — it launches the app as a black box.
- Add app code to tests with `@testable import YourApp` (unit tests only; gives access to `internal` symbols). UI tests use the accessibility layer, not imports.
- A `.xctestplan` lets you group tests, set env vars, and pick run configurations (e.g. randomized order). One default plan is fine for a prototype.
- Swift Testing and XCTest **coexist in the same target and same run** — migrate incrementally.

---

## Swift Testing (`@Test`) — the modern default

Import `Testing`, not `XCTest`. Tests are global functions or methods annotated `@Test`; assertions use `#expect` (non-fatal, keeps going) and `#require` (fatal, unwraps/stops).

```swift
import Testing
@testable import MyApp

@Test func totalIncludesTax() {
    let cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10), .init(price: 5)])
    #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0.1) == 16.5)
}
```

- `#expect(expr)` records a failure and **continues** — the macro captures sub-expression values, so a failure prints the actual operands (no need for XCTest-style messages).
- `#require(expr)` throws and **halts the test** on failure — use it for preconditions where continuing is pointless. It also unwraps optionals (call in a `throws` test with `try`):

```swift
@Test func parsesUser() throws {
    let user = try #require(User(json: validJSON))  // stops here if nil
    #expect(user.name == "Ada")
}
```

### Suites and shared setup

Group with a `struct` (preferred) or `final class`. A **fresh instance is created per test**, so `init` is your per-test setup — no shared mutable state between tests by default.

```swift
@Suite("Cart pricing")
struct CartTests {
    let cart: Cart              // built fresh for every @Test below

    init() { cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10)]) }

    @Test func emptyTaxIsIdentity() {
        #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0) == 10)
    }
}
```

Teardown: for a `struct` suite there usually is none — value types just drop when the instance goes away. If you genuinely need cleanup, use a `final class` and put it in `deinit`. Note `deinit` **cannot be `async` or `throwing`** and can't be actor-isolated, so for `@MainActor` suites or async cleanup, do the work at the end of each test (or use a custom scoping trait) rather than relying on `deinit`.

### Parameterized tests — one test, many cases

Replaces copy-pasted test bodies. Each argument runs as a **separate, independently-reported case**. A single array of tuples destructures positionally into multiple parameters:

```swift
@Test(arguments: [
    ("", false),
    ("a@b.co", true),
    ("no-at", false),
])
func validatesEmail(_ input: String, _ expected: Bool) {
    #expect(EmailValidator.isValid(input) == expected)
}
```

Destructuring is positional — element labels in the tuples don't have to match parameter names and are best omitted to avoid confusion. Cross-product of two sequences (every combination):

```swift
@Test(arguments: [1, 2, 3], ["x", "y"])   // 6 cases
func combos(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(!s.isEmpty && n > 0) }
```

Wrap in `zip(a, b)` when you want **paired** (not cross-product) cases:

```swift
@Test(arguments: zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b", "c"]))   // 3 cases
func paired(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(n > 0 && !s.isEmpty) }
```

### Traits: naming, tagging, skipping, known bugs

```swift
@Test("Discount never goes negative")                       // display name
@Test(.disabled("flaky until CI fix"))                      // skip, stays visible
@Test(.enabled(if: FeatureFlags.checkoutV2))                // conditional run
@Test(.bug("https://example.com/issue/42", "rounding"))     // url first, then title
@Test(.tags(.fast))                                         // group across files
```

Define tags once (do **not** add `@Test` — a tag is not a test):

```swift
extension Tag { @Tag static var fast: Self }
```

Run a subset from the CLI with `swift test --filter` / `xcodebuild ... -only-testing:`, or filter by tag in Xcode's Test navigator.

I am comfortable signing this as architecture-ready now, with one hard red-team add-on that must be locked before build: every request must carry a server-issued, monotonically increasing `requestRevision` and every action mutation call must include an optional `expectedRequestRevision` so the coordinator can reject stale local intent deterministically before it touches UI state. Concrete break: Device A is offline, queues `accept` for request R. Device B accepts and completes/reject/re-opens flows before A reconnects. Without an expected-revision guard, A can replay an outbox action against a terminalized row and briefly animate into a misleading state transition before fetch correction; with revision-aware CAS we force immediate `conflict`/`reconciling` and a fresh pull, preserving the no-ambiguous-outcome rule. This is a single concrete decision, not a "nice-to-have": action payloads now include revision intent, and the reducer only accepts action responses whose `requestRevision` can be reconciled in-order per request.

The architecture stays a one-service backend + thin SwiftUI client contract: custom REST `/api/v1` over PostgreSQL, no sockets, no third-party app deps, explicit CAS endpoints only. The core invariant is server truth plus client event reducer: cache may be stale, only server-confirmed transitions are final. On device, `AppSession` drives `AppGate` routing and owns signed-in user + active pod + board handle; `RequestSyncCoordinator` remains an actor and the only mutator of in-memory request phase transitions, fed by local user actions, refreshes, push wake signals, and deep-links. UI reads view models derived from pure domain state (no ad-hoc booleans). APNs is trigger-only: payload can name IDs, never authoritative truth.

I would structure modules as:
`pulse-relay/Sources/App` for app entry, routes, and gate; `.../Domain` for models, enums, reducers, and validation; `.../Services` for API client, auth, APNs registration, deep-link parsing, and sync orchestration; `.../Persistence` for SwiftData cache + durable outbox plus schema-safe recovery; `.../Features` for RelayBoard/Composer/Detail/Receipt/Profile/PodSettings views; `.../Tests` with unit tests in `@Test` plus one backend concurrency suite and one smoke UI test. This separation maps cleanly to `primary_ui`, `data_domain`, `services_utilities`, and `polish_resilience` lanes.

Data model is intentionally narrow and explicit: `User`, `Pod`, `PodMember`, `RelayRequest`, `RelayReceipt`, `ActionRecord`, `RequestRevision`, and `ActionPlan`/`ActionOutcome` value types. `RelayRequest` includes:
`state`, `serverRevision` (`UInt64`), `createdAtUtc`, `lastUpdatedUtc`, `podHomeTz`, `isMine`, `requesterAlias`, `note`, `isWithdrawnTerminal`, and `isReceiptAvailable`.  
The board contract is server-authoritative ordering by `createdAtUtc` + deterministic tie-break (`serverRevision`, `id`), then `displayOrder` for response stability. No client urgency ranking exists because there is no urgency field in scope. All timing user-facing text must use server epoch inputs and be rendered as `MM:SS` under one hour, then `Xh Ym` as defined.

Persistence strategy is split by correctness versus cache: SwiftData is cache-only for pod/request/receipt snapshots with invalidation policy on schema/version mismatch (purge + refetch from server); this is explicitly okay because source of truth is server. Outbox is not cache: `OutboxAction` is durable across launch and app-version upgrade and stores actionId, expectedRevision, action type, payload, createdAt, attempt counters, and terminal action result. On relaunch or upgrade conflict, stale cache can render for continuity only, but terminal states are blocked from green-state rendering until first successful sync. On any queued replay conflict, coordinator emits reconciling -> fetch -> settle, never local optimistic completion.  
Security/privacy/perms stay minimal: Sign in with Apple + Remote notifications only; no location/contacts/photos/camera; Keychain tokens with after-first-unlock accessibility; no notification action buttons; deep link + refetch to reconcile is the only post-push action path. Privacy manifest must include declared data collection for Keychain/notifications.

Testing strategy is two-tier and non-negotiable: backend concurrency acceptance tests hitting real test endpoint must verify deterministic CAS outcomes (`accept` races and `accept` vs `withdraw`) with idempotent action IDs and revision guards; and a two-device demo script (seeded pod + concurrent accept + loser branch + release/reopen + still-open escalation + force-quit resume). Unit tests prioritize reducer transitions (queuedOffline/awaiting/reconciling exclusivity), revision conflict handling, action-id dedupe, and elapsed timer/render contract. Network unit tests use stubbed URLProtocol with fixed payloads only; no real network in unit suite. A light SwiftData round-trip test verifies outbox survives store reset/recreate paths.

I also lock one architecture-level health requirement for this phase: a lightweight backend reachability call (`GET /api/v1/health`) must be part of initial client verification and must return `podOnboardingReady`, `apiRevision`, and `minClientVersion` so the app can hard-stop on unsupported protocol mismatch instead of silently proceeding with half-valid behavior.
